lead: Nadifloxacin is a topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for acne vulgaris and for bacterial skin infections. For appearance, it is used to calm inflamed pimples and pustules so the skin looks clearer and less red, often alongside a retinoid such as adapalene or with benzoyl peroxide.[1][2][3]

It is marketed as a 1% cream in Japan, parts of Europe and some Asian countries, and is not approved in the United States.[1][2] It works by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and is active in vitro against Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), Staphylococcus epidermidis and MRSA.[2]

Randomised trials in Japanese, Korean and other Asian patients report lesion reductions with nadifloxacin 1%, including a split-face trial against vehicle, a comparison with erythromycin gel, and a combination study with adapalene.[4][5][6] Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolone use could promote quinolone resistance.[2]

Acne is one of the most common reasons people seek skin treatment, and visible inflamed lesions are what most patients want gone. Nadifloxacin sits in the group of topical antibacterials aimed at that inflammatory component. Because it is a quinolone rather than a macrolide or lincosamide, it has been discussed by dermatologists as an alternative where resistance to erythromycin or clindamycin is a concern.[10][11]

chain: Apply nadifloxacin cream to acne-prone skin
Acne-associated bacteria are suppressed and inflammation falls
Fewer red, inflamed pimples; clearer-looking skin
angle.text: Patients use the cream to reduce inflammatory acne lesions. Dermatologists in countries where it is sold prescribe it on its own or combined with adapalene or benzoyl peroxide to clear inflamed spots faster.

paras: Grokipedia attributes development to Otsuka Pharmaceutical in Japan under the code OPC-7251 and reports a 1993 Japanese approval for acne vulgaris, with indications widened in 1998 to other superficial skin infections caused by susceptible bacteria.[1] Wikipedia lists it as approved for acne in some European countries and gives its brand names as Acuatim, Nadiflox, Nadoxin, Nadixa and Activon.[2] A 2021 pharmaceutical review groups it with levonadifloxacin and other quinolones approved since 2000, characterising its physicochemical properties, formulations and antibacterial spectrum.[12]

Early work on acne-associated bacteria showed that Cutibacterium acnes (then Propionibacterium acnes) is sensitive in vitro to a wide range of antimicrobials, nadifloxacin among them, although a 2001 review notes that drugs differ in how well they penetrate the lipid-filled microcomedo and lower bacterial numbers in the skin.[10]

Nadifloxacin is used for mild to moderate acne, where it targets the inflamed papules and pustules that drive redness and visible blemishes.[1][2] Grokipedia says it is often combined with benzoyl peroxide or adapalene.[1]

In the acne literature the cream is used in combination regimens. Trials have paired it with adapalene, with benzoyl peroxide and with tretinoin, and one registered Phase 3 study compared nadifloxacin cream alone against nadifloxacin with benzoyl peroxide solution.[3][6][13] Grokipedia describes a twice-daily regimen over 8 to 12 weeks, and reports a mean total-lesion fall from 26.8 to 8.2 over eight weeks in an assessor-blinded trial pairing it with benzoyl peroxide, similar to clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide; this account comes from an AI-generated page.[1]
It is also used for pyodermas such as impetigo and folliculitis.[1][2] A small study in young children examined it for atopic dermatitis complicated by MRSA.[7]

A randomised split-face trial in Korean patients with mild to moderate acne found inflammatory lesions fell by about 70 percent on the nadifloxacin-treated side while rising on the vehicle side, with histology showing reduced inflammation.[5]
A randomised comparison of 86 patients found nadifloxacin 1% cream and erythromycin 4% gel both reduced lesion counts and severity scores from week 4 through 12 weeks, with similar results.[4]

In a 12-week multicentre Japanese trial of 184 patients with moderate-to-severe acne, adding nadifloxacin 1% cream to adapalene 0.1% gel reduced inflammatory lesions significantly more than adapalene alone from week 4, and none of the 76 tested bacterial strains was resistant to nadifloxacin.[6]

Grokipedia also reports high clinical cure rates in pyodermas, quoting a pooled analysis of 272 patients with 97.8 percent cured by day 7 and a post-marketing series of 329 patients.[1] The studies behind those figures are not individually listed on that page.

Adverse reactions are mostly local: burning, itching (most common), contact dermatitis, dryness and irritation.[2] A 21-day patch study in 40 healthy volunteers found that nadifloxacin combined with adapalene, benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid or isotretinoin produced mostly zero irritation scores, all below 1.[8]

Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolone use could promote quinolone resistance.[2] Studies of acne bacteria have documented resistance to other topical antibiotics such as erythromycin and clindamycin in several countries.[9]

Resistance is the main safety discussion around topical antibiotics for acne. A 2016 meta-analysis of 13 articles reported a slight tendency toward resistance of C. acnes to topical erythromycin and clindamycin (mean odds ratio 1.24).[11] A Japanese hospital study examined the relationship between acne severity and antimicrobial resistance of bacteria cultured from lesions.[14] Authors of the Wikipedia entry note a view that quinolones should be held back from mild conditions such as acne because of resistance risk, whereas the Japanese combination trial found no resistant strains among the 76 it tested.[2][6] Grokipedia states that guidelines advise short application courses of 5 to 7 days for skin infections.[1]

It inhibits DNA gyrase, halting bacterial replication, and may have sebostatic and anti-inflammatory effects.[2] After a single large application of 1% cream, peak plasma level was 107 ng/mL with a half-life of 19.4 hours.[2]

Wikipedia describes in vitro activity against aerobic Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, with potency against MRSA similar to that against methicillin-susceptible strains and some activity against quinolone-resistant MRSA.[2] Because the cream is applied locally, systemic exposure is described as low compared with oral quinolones.[1]
It is a racemic fluoroquinolone, formula C19H21FN2O4, molar mass about 360.4 g/mol.[2]

Randomised trials include a split-face versus vehicle study in Korea,[5] a comparison with erythromycin gel,[4] a Japanese multicentre trial of nadifloxacin plus adapalene versus adapalene,[6] and an irritation study of combinations.[8] Grokipedia (AI-generated, less reliable) also describes comparisons with clindamycin combinations.[1] A registered phase 4 trial comparing nadifloxacin plus tretinoin with clindamycin plus tretinoin for mild-to-moderate acne is recruiting.[3]

The registered trials include a Phase 3 study of nadifloxacin cream alone versus with benzoyl peroxide solution (about 90 participants, start 2008, status unknown) and a Phase 4 study of nadifloxacin versus sisomicin cream in primary pyodermas that was withdrawn.[13] The 2026 Phase 4 trial of nadifloxacin plus tretinoin versus clindamycin plus tretinoin enrols 158 participants.[3]

The cream is sold under brand names such as Acuatim, Nadiflox, Nadoxin, Nadixa and Activon in the countries where it is approved, and the clinical literature on it comes largely from Japan, Korea and other Asian centres.[2][4][5][6] It is not approved in the United States.[1][2]

name: Nadifloxacin

card.summary: A topical quinolone antibiotic cream for acne used in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia but not the US.
card.note: Not US-approved; concern about quinolone resistance.

quick.overview:
Nadifloxacin is a 1% antibiotic cream for acne and skin infections, available in Japan, some European and Asian countries.

Small studies reportedly show lesion reductions comparable to clindamycin combinations, but evidence in the sources is limited.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, killing or stopping acne-related bacteria such as Cutibacterium acnes, and may have anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.risks: Mostly local burning, itching, dryness. Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolones could promote resistance. Not approved in the US.
